title: Market Basics
blurb: Shares, exchanges, orders, settlement and the charges on every trade.
source: Covers the same ground as the opening modules of Zerodha Varsity, written fresh for this app. Varsity is free and goes much deeper.

lessons.title: What you own when you buy a share
body: A company splits its ownership into equal pieces called **shares**. If a company has 100 crore shares and you hold one, you own one part in 100 crore of the business: a claim on its future profits and a vote at its meetings.

The price moves because buyers and sellers keep re-estimating what those future profits are worth. Over weeks, mood and news dominate. Over decades, the price tends to follow the growth in the company's earnings.

list: **Price gain:** you sell later for more than you paid.
**Dividends:** the company pays out part of its profit in cash.
**Loss:** the business disappoints, and the price can fall a long way, even to near zero.

body: An **ETF** (exchange-traded fund) is a basket you buy like a share. One unit of a Nifty 50 ETF such as NIFTYBEES gives you a small slice of all 50 companies in the index, in the same proportions as the index.

body.note: In this game every rupee is pretend money, but the mechanics are real: the same order types, the same charges, the same settlement rules.

lessons.takeaway: A share is a part of a real business. Before buying, ask whether you'd be happy to own that business for five years.

quiz.q: When you buy one share of a company, what do you own?
o: A loan you have given the company
A tiny part of the business
A deposit held by the exchange
A promise to buy more shares later
quiz.e: Shares are ownership. A loan to a company is a bond or debenture, which is a different instrument.

quiz.q: Over decades, what mainly drives a company's share price?
o: How many people own the stock
quiz.e: News moves prices in the short run. Over long periods, prices tend to track what the business earns.

quiz.q: What does one unit of a Nifty 50 ETF give you?
o: A slice of all 50 Nifty companies
A share of the best Nifty stock
quiz.e: An index ETF holds every company in its index, so one unit spreads your money across all of them.

lessons.title: Who's who: SEBI, exchanges, depositories, brokers
body: Four kinds of institution sit behind every trade you place.

list: **Exchanges (NSE, BSE)** run the order books where buy and sell orders meet and get matched electronically.
**SEBI** is the regulator. It writes the rules for exchanges, brokers and mutual funds and handles investor complaints.
**Depositories (CDSL, NSDL)** hold your shares electronically in your **demat account**, in your name.
**Your broker** sends your orders to the exchange and usually also acts as your **depository participant (DP)**, the link between you and the depository.

body: A **clearing corporation** stands in the middle of every trade and guarantees it settles, so you never depend on the honesty of the unknown person on the other side.

Because shares sit in your name at the depository, they can't leave your demat without your permission. That's why a sale asks for your CDSL TPIN and an OTP, unless you have signed a one-time authorisation called DDPI.

It's also why the **DP charge** exists. Each time shares leave your demat on a sale, the depository and your DP charge a flat fee per stock. At Zerodha it is ₹15.34 per stock per day, whatever the quantity.
lessons.takeaway: Your shares belong to you at the depository, not to your broker. The flat DP charge on sales comes from that arrangement.

quiz.q: Where are your shares actually held?
o: In your demat account at a depository
quiz.e: CDSL and NSDL hold shares electronically in your name. The broker is only your participant in that system.

quiz.q: Who regulates India's securities markets?
quiz.e: SEBI regulates securities markets. RBI regulates banks and monetary policy.

quiz.q: Why does selling ask for a TPIN and OTP?
o: To authorise shares leaving your demat
quiz.e: The depository needs your permission before shares leave your account. DDPI is a standing version of that permission.

lessons.title: Order types: market, limit and after-hours
body: When you place an order you choose how it should be filled.

list: **Market order:** fill now at the best price available. It's fast but you don't control the price.
**Limit order:** you name the worst price you'll accept. A buy limit at ₹250 fills only at ₹250 or lower, and it may never fill.
**After-market order (AMO):** placed while the market is closed and sent to the exchange when the next session opens.

body: Every stock has a **bid** (the highest price buyers offer) and an **ask** (the lowest price sellers want). The gap is the **spread**. For busy stocks it's a few paise. For thinly traded ETFs it can be much wider, and a market order pays the whole gap. Limit orders protect you there.

Orders are also either **delivery** (CNC: the shares come into your demat and you can hold them for years) or **intraday** (MIS: borrowed buying power, closed the same day). This game uses delivery only, because that's how investing works.
NSE's normal session runs **9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST** on trading days, with a short pre-open session from 9:00 am.
lessons.takeaway: Use limit orders when the spread is wide or the price matters to you. Market orders are fine for very liquid stocks and ETFs.

quiz.q: A stock trades at ₹255. You place a buy limit at ₹250. What happens?
o: It waits and fills only if the price reaches ₹250 or lower
quiz.e: A limit sets the worst price you accept. Until a seller offers ₹250 or less, the order waits.

quiz.q: Why prefer a limit order for a thinly traded ETF?
o: A wide bid-ask spread can make a market order fill at a poor price
Market orders aren't allowed for ETFs
quiz.e: Thin trading means a wide spread. A market order buys at whatever the best ask is, even if it's far above fair value.

quiz.q: When does NSE's normal trading session run?
quiz.e: The normal session is 9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST, with a pre-open session from 9:00 am.

lessons.title: After you tap Buy: settlement and charges
body: Indian equities settle on **T+1**: shares you buy today arrive in your demat on the next trading day, and money from a sale arrives the next trading day too.
The same day you get a **contract note**, the legal bill for the trade. It lists the price, the quantity and every charge. Delivery charges at a typical discount broker look like this:

list: **Brokerage:** often ₹0 for delivery.
**STT (securities transaction tax):** 0.1% on both buy and sell for shares. Most equity ETFs pay 0.001% on the sell side only. Gold and liquid ETFs pay none.
**Exchange transaction charges and the SEBI fee:** tiny percentages of the trade value.
**Stamp duty:** 0.015% on purchases.
**GST:** 18% on brokerage plus exchange and SEBI charges.
**DP charge:** a flat fee on every sale, per stock per day. ₹15.34 at Zerodha.

slip.title: Buy and later sell ₹10,000 of a stock

body: Now shrink the trade. A ₹1,000 round trip costs about ₹17.56, or 1.76%, mostly the DP charge. Selling a single ₹120 ETF unit loses about 13% to that one flat fee.
lessons.takeaway: Flat fees punish small sales. Buy in sensible sizes and sell rarely.

quiz.q: You sell shares on a Monday that is a trading day. When does the money settle?
quiz.e: India moved to T+1 settlement for equities, so the money settles the next trading day.

quiz.q: Which charge is a flat amount rather than a percentage of the trade?
quiz.e: The DP charge is per stock per day, whatever the quantity. That's why it hurts small sales most.

quiz.q: Which of these ETFs pays no STT?
quiz.e: Gold and liquid ETFs pay no STT. Most equity ETFs pay 0.001% on the sell side.

quiz.q: Roughly what does a ₹10,000 stock round trip cost in charges with zero brokerage?
quiz.e: STT on both sides (₹20), the DP charge (₹15.34) and small fees add up to about ₹37.56.

lessons.title: Indices: Nifty 50 and friends
body: An **index** tracks a basket of stocks to measure part of the market. The **Nifty 50** follows 50 large companies listed on NSE. It started at 1,000 points in November 1995.
Each company's weight comes from its **free-float market capitalisation**: the value of the shares available to the public, leaving out promoter holdings. Bigger companies move the index more.

list: **Nifty Next 50:** the next 50 companies by size. Bumpier, and the place future Nifty 50 members often come from.
**Sensex:** BSE's 30-stock index.
**Nifty Bank:** the largest banking stocks.

body: Index points aren't rupees. If the Nifty is at 23,000 and falls 230 points, that's a 1% fall. The percentage is what matters.
NSE reviews index membership twice a year. Index funds and ETFs copy these changes so you don't have to do anything.
lessons.takeaway: Read index moves in percent, not points. A broad index is the simplest way to own a diversified piece of India Inc.

quiz.q: How does the Nifty 50 weight its companies?
quiz.e: Weights follow the market value of freely traded shares, so the largest companies have the most influence.

quiz.q: The Nifty is at 23,000 and falls 230 points. What is the percentage change?
Compared with the Nifty 50, the Nifty Next 50 is usually:
quiz.e: Smaller companies tend to swing more, so the Next 50 is typically bumpier.

title: Index Investing
blurb: Why owning the whole market cheaply is hard to beat, and how ETFs and gold fit in.
source: Introduces ideas John C. Bogle argued for in The Little Book of Common Sense Investing, applied to India and written in our own words. Read the book for his full case.

links.label: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (book)

lessons.title: Own the whole haystack
body: John Bogle founded Vanguard and in 1976 launched the first index fund for ordinary investors. His central argument: rather than hunting for the few stocks that will win, own the entire market at the lowest possible cost and hold it.

The reasoning is arithmetic. All investors together own the whole market, so **before costs** the average rupee invested must earn the market's return. **After costs** (fees, trading, taxes) the average investor has to earn less. The index investor pays the least, so keeps the most.
This doesn't depend on fund managers being unskilled. Some will beat the market, but picking them in advance is hard, and many winners don't stay winners.
Indian data agrees. S&P's SPIVA India scorecard for year-end 2025 found that about **76% of large-cap funds** trailed their benchmark over 10 years.

body.note: What you give up with an index fund is the chance to beat the market. What you gain is near-certainty of getting close to the market's return.

lessons.takeaway: Before costs, investing is a zero-sum split of the market's return. After costs, the cheapest participant comes out ahead.

quiz.q: Before costs, the average investor's return equals:
o: The return of the best fund
quiz.e: All investors together are the market, so on average they earn exactly its return before costs.

quiz.q: Why must the average active investor trail the market after costs?
o: They pay more costs out of the same average return
quiz.e: Same average return before costs, higher costs, so a lower return after costs.

quiz.q: Per SPIVA India year-end 2025, about what share of large-cap funds trailed their benchmark over 10 years?
quiz.e: About 76% of large-cap funds underperformed over 10 years.

lessons.title: Costs compound too
body: Returns compound, and so do costs. A 1% yearly fee sounds tiny, but it's taken from your whole balance every year, including everything it has already grown into.

slip.title: ₹10,000 a month for 25 years (₹30 lakh invested)

body: In India the same fund often comes in two plans. A **regular plan** includes a distributor's commission. A **direct plan** doesn't, so its expense ratio is lower. The portfolio inside is identical.
Many index funds charge well under 0.5% a year, while regular plans of active funds often charge 1.5% or more. Check the expense ratio (TER) on the fund's factsheet.
Costs also hide outside the expense ratio: bid-ask spreads, STT and DP charges on frequent trades, and tax every time you sell at a gain.
lessons.takeaway: You can't control returns, but you can control costs. Every 1% saved compounds in your favour.

quiz.q: Over 25 years of ₹10,000 a month, how much does an extra 1% yearly cost shrink the final value?
quiz.e: ₹1.70 crore at 12% against ₹1.45 crore at 11%: about 15% less.

quiz.q: How does a direct plan differ from a regular plan of the same fund?
o: It has a lower expense ratio because no commission is paid
It can only be bought offline
quiz.e: Same portfolio. The regular plan pays a distributor commission out of the fund's expenses.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hidden cost of frequent trading?
quiz.e: Each round trip pays STT, and each sale pays a DP charge, on top of any tax on gains.

lessons.title: ETF or index mutual fund?
body: Both track an index. They differ in how you buy them.

list: **ETF:** trades on the exchange through your demat account, like a share. The price moves during the day. You pay STT and DP charges, and you need someone on the other side to trade with.
**Index mutual fund:** you buy from the fund house at the day's closing NAV. No demat needed, no DP charge, automatic SIPs are easy. Expense ratios are often slightly higher than the cheapest ETFs.

body: An ETF's market price can drift from the value of what it holds. That value, updated live during market hours, is called the **iNAV** (indicative NAV) and is published by the fund house. If the ETF trades at ₹265 while its iNAV is ₹261, buying means paying a premium of about 1.5%.
**Tracking difference** is how far the fund's return falls short of the index over a year. Lower is better.

body.note: A simple rule: for automatic monthly investing, an index fund SIP is easiest. ETFs suit occasional purchases if you check liquidity and iNAV and use limit orders.

lessons.takeaway: Before buying an ETF, compare its price with its iNAV and use a limit order.

quiz.q: What does an ETF's iNAV tell you?
o: The live value of the ETF's underlying holdings
quiz.e: iNAV is the indicative value of what the ETF holds, updated during market hours.

quiz.q: An ETF trades at ₹265 while its iNAV is ₹261. Buying now means:
quiz.e: (265 − 261) ÷ 261 ≈ 1.5% above the value of the holdings.

quiz.q: Which of the two needs a demat account?
quiz.e: ETFs trade on the exchange and settle into your demat. Mutual fund units don't need one.

lessons.title: Where gold fits
body: A **gold ETF** holds physical gold of high purity in a vault, and each unit represents a small fraction of a gram.

Gold earns no profits or interest. Its return comes only from price changes. It has often moved differently from shares and has tended to hold up in crises, which is why it's used as a **diversifier** rather than a main growth engine. Many planners suggest a modest slice, often in the 5–15% range.
In India, gold's rupee price also reflects the exchange rate. When the rupee weakens against the dollar, gold in rupees tends to rise.

list: **STT:** none on gold ETFs.
**Tax:** held more than 12 months, gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation. Held 12 months or less, they're added to your income and taxed at your slab rate.

body: Holding two different gold ETFs adds nothing. They track the same metal, so it's the same bet twice, with an extra DP charge whenever you sell both.
lessons.takeaway: Treat gold as ballast for the portfolio, sized deliberately, and hold one fund for it.

quiz.q: Gold's usual role in a long-term portfolio is:
o: A replacement for an emergency fund
quiz.e: Gold produces no earnings. It earns its place by behaving differently from equities.

quiz.q: What do two different gold ETFs give you?
quiz.e: Both track the price of gold. Extra funds only add extra sale charges.

quiz.q: How is a gain on a gold ETF held for 14 months taxed?
quiz.e: Over 12 months counts as long term for listed gold ETFs, taxed at 12.5% without indexation.

lessons.title: Stay the course
body: Bogle's other theme was discipline. Index investing pays off only if you keep holding through the bad years.
Studies of fund flows repeatedly find that investors earn less than the funds they own. People tend to buy after prices have risen and sell after they have fallen, which is the reverse of what works.

list: Automate a monthly SIP so investing doesn't depend on your mood.
Review once or twice a year, not daily.
Rebalance when your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target.
Ignore forecasts. Nobody reliably knows next month's market.

body: In this game, fast-forward the simulated market through a few bad months without selling and watch what happens to your account.
lessons.takeaway: The plan you can stick with beats the clever plan you abandon in a crash.

quiz.q: Why do investors often earn less than the funds they own?
o: They buy after rises and sell after falls
quiz.e: Chasing performance and panic selling move money in at high prices and out at low ones.

quiz.q: A sensible review schedule for a long-term portfolio is:
quiz.e: Frequent checking invites action. A scheduled review keeps the plan on track.

quiz.q: When is rebalancing usually considered?
o: When your mix drifts about 5 points from target
When a friend gives a tip
quiz.e: A drift band avoids constant small trades while keeping risk where you chose it.

title: Money Foundations
blurb: Emergency fund, insurance, goals, allocation and tax: the groundwork before investing.
source: Introduces personal-finance themes that Monika Halan's Let's Talk Money is known for in India, such as getting the foundations right before chasing returns, written in our own words. Read the book for her full system.

lessons.title: The order of operations
body: Investing is the fourth step, not the first.

list: **1. A cash buffer.** Know what you spend, and build an emergency fund.
**2. Insurance.** Health cover for yourself, and term life cover if anyone depends on your income.
**3. Expensive debt.** Credit-card balances often cost over 30% a year. No investment reliably beats that.
**4. Investing** for goals.

body: The order matters because without a buffer, a job loss or a hospital bill forces you to sell investments at whatever price the market offers that week, often a bad one.

A simple structure helps: salary lands in one account, and on payday fixed amounts move automatically to a spending account and to investments. Investing first and spending what's left beats saving whatever is left over.
lessons.takeaway: Buffer, insurance, expensive debt, then investing. Skipping ahead makes every market fall a personal crisis.

quiz.q: Which comes first?
quiz.e: A cash buffer keeps emergencies from forcing you to sell investments at a bad time.

quiz.q: Why pay off a credit-card balance before investing?
o: Its interest often exceeds 30% a year
quiz.e: Clearing a 30%+ debt is a guaranteed 30%+ return. No investment offers that reliably.

quiz.q: What does paying yourself first mean?
o: Spending first and saving the remainder
Moving money to investments on payday, before spending
quiz.e: Automating the investment on payday makes saving the default.

lessons.title: Building the emergency fund
body: An emergency fund covers essential expenses if income stops or a big bill arrives. A common guide is **six months of essential spending**: more if your income is irregular or people depend on you, less while you're a student with low fixed costs.
It must be **safe and quick to reach**:

list: A savings account or a sweep-in fixed deposit.
A liquid mutual fund or liquid ETF, which hold very short-term debt.
Not shares, equity funds or gold, which can be down 20–40% exactly when you need the money.

body: The emergency fund's job is to be there, not to earn much. A lower return is the price of certainty.

body.note: In this game, LIQUIDBEES stands in for the emergency-fund bucket. The real LIQUIDBEES stays near ₹1,000 and pays its return as extra units. Here it's shown as a slowly rising price to keep things simple.

lessons.takeaway: Six months of essentials, kept somewhere boring and reachable.

quiz.q: A common guide for emergency-fund size is:
quiz.e: Around six months of essentials, adjusted for how stable your income is.

quiz.q: Which is a poor place for an emergency fund?
quiz.e: Stocks can fall sharply just when you need the money.

quiz.q: What is the emergency fund's main job?
o: Beating inflation by a wide margin
quiz.e: Certainty and access come before returns.

lessons.title: Insurance is not an investment
body: Insurance moves a risk you can't afford onto an insurer. Investing grows money. Mixing the two usually does both badly.

list: **Term life insurance** pays only if you die during the term. Premiums are low, so large cover is affordable. A commonly suggested size is 10–15 times your annual income, if someone depends on that income.
**Health insurance** protects your savings from hospital bills. Employer cover ends when the job does, so a personal policy matters too.

body: **Endowment, money-back and many ULIP policies** combine cover with investment. They tend to offer small cover, high costs, long lock-ins and modest returns. A common alternative is to buy term cover and invest the difference yourself.
A student with no dependants usually doesn't need life cover yet, but does benefit from health cover.
lessons.takeaway: Buy insurance for protection and investments for growth, separately.

quiz.q: What does term life insurance do?
o: Pays a guaranteed return at maturity
Pays only if the insured person dies during the term
quiz.e: Term cover is pure protection, which is why it's cheap.

quiz.q: Why are endowment-style policies often criticised?
o: Small cover, high costs and modest returns
quiz.e: Mixing cover with investment tends to shortchange both.

quiz.q: Who most needs term life cover?
o: Someone whose income others depend on
A retired person with no dependants
quiz.e: Life cover replaces income for dependants. With no dependants, the need is small.

lessons.title: Goals and time horizons
body: Match each rupee to when you'll need it.

list: **Under 3 years** (a laptop, a course fee): fixed deposits, liquid or short-term debt funds. Equity is too unpredictable over this span.
**3–7 years** (a car, a home down payment): a mix of debt and equity.
**7+ years** (retirement, long-term wealth): mostly diversified equity, such as index funds.

body: Equity markets have fallen 30–60% in bad years. Money needed next year shouldn't be exposed to that. Money needed in 15 years has time to recover.
Write each goal as an **amount and a date**: "₹6 lakh down payment by March 2030" is a goal. "Get rich" isn't.
lessons.takeaway: The date you need the money decides where it should sit.

quiz.q: Money you need in 18 months is best kept in:
o: Fixed deposits or a short-term debt fund
quiz.e: Short horizons can't ride out an equity crash.

quiz.q: Which is a well-defined goal?
quiz.e: An amount and a date let you plan the monthly saving and the right product.

quiz.q: Why does a long horizon suit equity?
o: There's time to recover from falls
Equity never falls over long periods
quiz.e: Equity can fall hard, but long horizons have historically given it time to recover.

lessons.title: Asset allocation and rebalancing
body: **Asset allocation** is your split between equity, debt and gold. It decides most of how your portfolio behaves: how far it can fall and how fast it can grow.
Choose a split you could hold through a crash. An 80% equity portfolio feels fine in a boom. In a 40% market fall it drops about 32%. Ask yourself honestly whether you'd stay put.

Markets move your mix away from target over time. **Rebalancing** brings it back. The cheapest way is to point new money at whatever is underweight, which avoids sale charges and tax. Selling the overweight part is the fallback when drift is large.

body.note: Set a target allocation in the Portfolio tab. The game then shows your drift and what new money would bring you back to target.

lessons.takeaway: Pick a mix you'll keep in bad times, then steer back to it with new money.

quiz.q: An 80% equity portfolio faces a 40% market fall. Roughly how much does the portfolio fall?
quiz.e: 80% × 40% = 32%, assuming the other 20% holds steady.

quiz.q: What's the cheapest way to rebalance?
o: Direct new money to the underweight asset
quiz.e: Buying the underweight asset needs no sale, so no DP charge and no capital gains tax.

quiz.q: What does asset allocation mainly decide?
o: How the portfolio behaves, including how far it can fall
quiz.e: The equity, debt and gold mix drives most of the ride.

lessons.title: Tax on your investments
body: India taxes gains when you sell. These were the rates for listed shares, equity funds and ETFs as of 2026:

list: **Held more than 12 months (long term):** 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year.
**Held 12 months or less (short term):** 20%.
**Gold ETFs:** 12.5% if held more than 12 months, otherwise added to your income at your slab rate.

body: Losses help. Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short- and long-term gains. Long-term losses only against long-term gains. Unused losses carry forward for 8 years if you file your return on time.
Because tax is charged on selling, a buy-and-hold investor defers tax for years, while a frequent trader pays it every time, at the higher short-term rate.

body.note: Budgets change these rules. Check the current rates on the Income Tax Department's site or with a CA before acting.

lessons.takeaway: Holding longer than 12 months lowers the rate and lets the first ₹1.25 lakh of yearly long-term equity gains go untaxed.

quiz.q: You sell equity ETF units after 8 months at a gain. Which rate applies?
quiz.e: 12 months or less counts as short term for listed equity: 20%.

quiz.q: Long-term equity gains up to what amount per year are untaxed?
quiz.e: The first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term equity gains in a financial year is exempt.

quiz.q: A long-term capital loss can be set off against:
quiz.e: Long-term losses offset only long-term gains. Short-term losses can offset both kinds.

title: Your Brain on Markets
blurb: Volatility, loss aversion, tips and leverage: why behaviour matters more than stock picking.
source: Draws on well-documented behavioural research and SEBI data.

lessons.title: Volatility is the price of admission
body: Daily swings of 1% in the Nifty are routine. A red "Day's P&L" is the normal texture of owning equities, not a signal.

Bigger falls happen too. In 2008 the Nifty fell roughly 60% from its peak. In early 2020 it fell almost 40% in about two months. In both cases it later climbed back above its old high: by late 2010 after the 2008 crash, and by late 2020 after the Covid fall.

**Volatility isn't the same as permanent loss.** For a diversified index, losses become permanent mainly when you sell near the bottom. For a single company, they can become permanent if the business fails.
Expected returns from equity exist precisely because the ride is uncomfortable. Without volatility there would be no premium for bearing it.
lessons.takeaway: Expect falls of 10–20% every few years and occasionally far worse. Plan for them before they happen.

quiz.q: Roughly how far did the Nifty fall from peak in 2008?
quiz.e: It fell roughly 60% from its early-2008 peak before recovering.

quiz.q: For a diversified index, when do losses usually become permanent?
o: When the price dips for a day
When you sell near the bottom
quiz.e: A broad index has historically recovered. Selling at the low turns a temporary fall into a realised loss.

quiz.q: Why does equity offer higher expected returns than a fixed deposit?
o: Investors are paid for bearing the swings
quiz.e: The extra return compensates for the discomfort and uncertainty.

lessons.title: Checking too often
body: Look at an equity portfolio daily and you'll see a loss on many of those days. Look once a year and losses show up far less often, because the long-term upward drift has time to outweigh the noise.

Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky documented **loss aversion**: a loss feels roughly twice as bad as an equal gain feels good. More looking means more pain, and more pain pushes people to act.
Acting usually means selling, which brings charges, tax and the risk of missing the recovery.

list: Turn off price notifications for long-term holdings.
Pick review dates and look then.
Judge the plan on years, not days.

lessons.takeaway: The less often you look, the better your decisions tend to be.

quiz.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Feeling losses more strongly than equal gains
quiz.e: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains please, which pushes people to over-react.

quiz.q: Checking a portfolio more often tends to:
o: Show more losses and invite more trading
quiz.e: Short windows are noisy, so you see more red, and that urges action.

quiz.q: A healthier habit is to:
quiz.e: Scheduled reviews keep you engaged without reacting to noise.

lessons.title: Tips, FOMO and F&O
body: Futures and options (F&O) let you trade large positions with a small margin. Leverage magnifies gains and losses equally, and the losses come fast.
SEBI's own studies are blunt. In FY2024-25, **91% of individual traders in equity F&O lost money**. An earlier study found 93% lost money over the three years to FY2024.

Tips follow the same logic. If someone had a reliable way to know which stock would rise, they wouldn't share it free in a group chat. Many "hot tips" exist so that the person sharing can sell to the people buying.
**FOMO** (fear of missing out) is strongest after a big rally, exactly when prices are least attractive.
lessons.takeaway: When something promises fast money, ask who's on the other side of the trade.

quiz.q: Per SEBI's study, what share of individual equity F&O traders lost money in FY2024-25?
quiz.e: SEBI found 91% lost money that year.

quiz.q: What does leverage do?
quiz.e: Borrowed exposure scales both directions.

quiz.q: When is FOMO usually strongest?
quiz.e: Rising prices create the urge to jump in, often near short-term highs.

lessons.title: Diversification and position size
body: Individual companies can collapse. Yes Bank shares, for example, lost more than 90% of their value between 2018 and 2020. Investors who'd put most of their money into one such stock never recovered that money.
**Diversification** means no single holding can wreck your plan. An index ETF does this automatically across 50 companies.
If you do buy individual stocks, many investors cap any one at around 5–10% of the portfolio, so that even a total loss stays survivable.
Diversification also means across asset classes (equity, debt, gold), not across many funds that all hold the same large companies.
lessons.takeaway: Size every bet so that being completely wrong is survivable.

quiz.q: What does diversification protect against most?
o: One holding wrecking the whole portfolio
quiz.e: It spreads company-specific risk. It doesn't remove market-wide falls.

quiz.q: Owning five large-cap funds that hold the same stocks gives you:
o: Lower risk than one index fund
quiz.e: Overlapping holdings mean the same exposure in different wrappers.

quiz.q: A common cap for any single stock is about:
quiz.e: Small position sizes keep a single failure survivable.

lessons.title: Time in the market vs timing it
body: Many of the market's best days arrive close to its worst days, in the middle of panics. An investor who jumps out to avoid the falls often misses the rebounds as well.
Waiting for the perfect entry has a cost of its own: while cash waits, it earns little and misses the market's growth.

Studies of US data, such as Charles Schwab's well-known comparison of investors with perfect and terrible timing, found that even perfect timing beat simply investing straight away by a surprisingly small margin. Staying in cash was by far the worst choice.

body.note: Don't take that on trust. The Lab tab lets you test it yourself on Nifty data: a monthly SIP against a dip-buyer, a perfect timer and a worst timer.

lessons.takeaway: Consistent investing usually beats waiting for the right moment.

quiz.q: Why does jumping out of the market to dodge falls often backfire?
o: The best days often follow the worst ones
quiz.e: Rebounds cluster near crashes, so leaving often means missing them.

quiz.q: What did studies of perfect versus immediate investing find?
o: Perfect timing won by a huge margin
Perfect timing won by a surprisingly small margin
quiz.e: Perfect timing helped only a little, and nobody can time perfectly in real life.

quiz.q: Where can you test this in the app?
quiz.e: The Lab runs these strategies on Nifty data.

title: The Data Project
blurb: Test SIP against market timing on Nifty data, then rebuild it in Python.
source: A hands-on project. Run it in the Lab, then reproduce it with the Python script included with the Android project.

lessons.title: Project brief: SIP vs timing
body: **Question:** does trying to time the market beat a plain monthly SIP in the Nifty?
**Method:** every strategy gets the same money, ₹10,000 at the start of each month, over the same period. Only the timing of purchases differs.

list: **Monthly SIP:** invest every month, no thinking.
**Dip buyer:** hold cash until the index is at least X% below its previous high, then invest everything saved.
**Perfect timer:** with hindsight, invests each month's money at the lowest point of that calendar year.
**Worst timer:** invests each month's money at the highest point of that calendar year.
**Cash only:** never invests, earns interest on cash.
**Lump sum:** invests the total on day one (a different question, shown for reference).

body: **Metrics:** final value, **XIRR** (the annual return that accounts for when each rupee went in) and the worst fall in portfolio value.
lessons.takeaway: Hold everything constant except the one thing you're testing.

quiz.q: Why does every strategy get the same monthly money?
o: So only timing differs between them
quiz.e: Controlling the inputs isolates the effect of timing.

quiz.q: What does XIRR account for?
quiz.e: XIRR weights returns by the timing of each cash flow.

quiz.q: The 'perfect timer' is:
o: A real strategy you can follow
A hindsight benchmark nobody can follow
quiz.e: It uses future knowledge, so it sets the upper limit of what timing could add.

lessons.title: Reading your results
body: After you run the Lab, look at three things.

list: **Gap between SIP and the perfect timer.** That gap is the most timing could ever have added, using knowledge no one has.
**Dip buyer's months in cash.** Waiting has a cost. In long bull runs the dip buyer may sit out for years.
**The worst fall.** Every equity strategy has one. Could you have held through it?

body: Then change one input at a time: the dip threshold, the start year, the cash interest rate. A finding that flips with small changes isn't robust.

Note what the data doesn't include: dividends (the Nifty price index leaves them out, worth roughly 1–1.5% a year), charges and taxes. These affect all strategies, so the comparison still holds, but absolute returns are understated.
lessons.takeaway: Judge a strategy by how much it really adds and how robust that is to small changes.

quiz.q: What does the SIP-to-perfect-timer gap measure?
o: The maximum value timing could add
quiz.e: Perfect hindsight sets the ceiling on timing benefits.

quiz.q: A result that changes when you tweak the start year slightly is:
quiz.e: Robust findings survive small changes in assumptions.

quiz.q: What does the Nifty price index leave out?
quiz.e: The price index excludes dividends. The Total Return Index includes them.

lessons.title: Take it further in Python
body: The Android project comes with **dalal_dojo_lab.py**, which repeats the Lab in Python with pandas, so you can extend it.

list: **Step-up SIP:** raise the monthly amount by 10% a year and compare.
**Rolling returns:** compute every 10-year SIP window and plot the spread of outcomes, not just one.
**Add gold:** blend GOLDBEES with the Nifty and test rebalancing yearly against never.
**Use total return data:** download the Nifty 50 TRI from niftyindices.com to include dividends.

body: A good write-up states the question, the data and its limits, the method, the result, and what would change your mind. That's also how a research paper is structured.
lessons.takeaway: Turn the Lab into a small study: one question, clear data, honest limits.

quiz.q: What do rolling returns show that one backtest doesn't?
o: The range of outcomes across many start dates
quiz.e: Many windows show how much results depend on luck of timing.

quiz.q: Which index includes dividends?
quiz.e: The TRI reinvests dividends, so it reflects what an investor actually earned.

quiz.q: A good study write-up should include:
quiz.e: Stating limits honestly is part of good analysis.
